opus-5.5.text:
I'd describe 3.7 as a watershed less because of any single benchmark number and more because of what it revealed about how post-training was evolving, at least from where I sat.

Before that, much of post-training was about shaping behavior: making the model helpful, harmless, following instructions well, having a good personality. That work was very important, but it was mostly about the model's style and judgment in a single response. Around 3.7, the emphasis shifted toward letting the model actually *do* things over longer horizons. That meant extended thinking, where the model can reason before answering, and much more serious work on agentic coding, where the model has to operate in a real environment, run tools, read errors, and iterate.

That shift changed the nature of the work. When your goal is "write a nice answer," you can lean heavily on human preference signals. When your goal is "fix this bug in a real repository," preference isn't really the right signal anymore. You need environments, verifiable outcomes, and reinforcement learning at a scale where the model learns from its own attempts. So post-training started looking less like polishing and more like building training grounds. The quality and diversity of environments, and how robust your reward is against the model finding shortcuts, became central questions.

It also exposed new problems that only show up once you push RL hard. For example, a model that's very eager to make tests pass might special-case the test instead of solving the problem. That's a reward-hacking issue, and you only see it clearly when the model becomes capable and persistent enough to find those paths. Learning to detect and suppress that kind of behavior became a big part of the following iterations.

So for me the watershed was conceptual: 3.7 was the point where it became clear that the frontier of post-training is agentic, long-horizon, RL-driven capability, and that coding is the most natural proving ground for it. A lot of what came afterward built directly on that realization.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier single-response behavior shaping and polishing with long-horizon, environment-based RL at scale, communicating a shift toward scalable post-training.

r002.rationale: It does not say the earlier approach was limited because Anthropic lacked a known way to scale post-training.

r003.rationale: It names verifiable outcomes and robust rewards as important signals for training models through their attempts in environments.

r004.rationale: It describes environments as training grounds and emphasizes their quality and diversity, but does not identify the environment itself as a strong data source.

fable-5.1.text:
I think 3.7 was the moment Anthropic's post-training stopped being mainly about making the model a better conversationalist and started being about making it a better agent.

Before that, most of the RL effort across the industry, including at Anthropic, was still oriented around single-turn quality. You optimize for a good answer, a helpful tone, maybe some math or coding benchmarks. The model is a very good responder. But a responder is not an agent. An agent has to decide what to do next, act in an environment, look at what comes back, and keep going for a long time without a human nudging it at each step.

With 3.7 you could feel that shift. The extended thinking was the visible part, but the more important thing was that the training environments themselves changed. The model was being trained in long-horizon, tool-using settings, especially coding, where the reward comes at the end of many steps rather than after one response. Once you do that, a lot of the old post-training recipe stops being sufficient. You need environments that are rich enough, verifiers that are reliable enough, and you have to accept that a lot of what the model learns is about process, not just about the final answer.

That is also why I call it a watershed rather than just an improvement. Benchmarks went up, yes, but the more consequential change was organizational and philosophical. It made the question "what environments are we training in" the central question, which I think is the right question for this era. Pre-training scaled on data. Post-training is going to scale on environments and on reward signals that actually reflect what we want agents to do in the world. 3.7 was the first Anthropic model where that bet was clearly visible from the outside, and everything after it follows that trajectory.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from single-turn response quality toward long-horizon agent training, but does not characterize it as a transition from small-scale model patching to scalable post-training.

r002.rationale: It does not say earlier post-training was limited because there was no known way to scale it.

r003.rationale: It names reliable verifiers and reward signals that reflect desired agent behavior, communicating the need for usable feedback signals.

r004.rationale: It says post-training will scale on environments, but does not identify the environment itself as a strong data source.

astra-6.text:
I think Claude 3.7 marked a shift in what post-training could accomplish. Earlier, you might think of post-training mainly as making a pretrained model more helpful—better at following instructions, answering questions, and matching human preferences. With 3.7, the interesting question became: can you train the model to spend additional computation working through a problem, and turn that computation into better performance?

The combination of ordinary responses and extended thinking made that shift very visible. But for me, the bigger implication was for coding and agents. Those tasks require more than a good next answer. You need to make a plan, take an action, inspect the result, and recover when something goes wrong. Post-training increasingly has to improve that whole process.

So I would call it a watershed in the direction of the work, rather than claim we know exactly what changed internally at Anthropic. The emphasis moved toward training models to solve problems over longer trajectories. That makes the training environments, the feedback, and the way you measure success much more central.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward longer problem-solving trajectories, but does not characterize it as a transition from small-scale model patching to scalable post-training.

r002.rationale: It does not say earlier post-training was limited because no way to scale it was known.

r003.rationale: It says feedback becomes more central, but does not identify sufficiently clear feedback signals as a requirement for scaling post-training.

r004.rationale: It mentions training environments as important, but does not identify the environment itself as a strong data source.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得关键不只是 Claude 3.7 的能力变强了，而是它把 reasoning 变成了一个可以通过 post-training 系统性提升的能力。以前大家谈 Claude，更多是在谈它的语言、写作，或者交互体验；到了 3.7，你会明显感觉到，它开始通过更长时间的思考来完成更难的任务，尤其是 coding 这种既需要推理、又比较容易获得反馈的任务。

这背后的变化是，post-training 不再只是让模型更好地回答问题、符合人的偏好，而是在继续扩展模型能解决的问题范围。训练时怎么利用可验证的反馈，推理时怎么分配计算量，这两件事开始连起来了。

当然，我们看不到 Anthropic 内部完整的训练过程，所以不能仅凭产品表现断言它具体用了什么方法。但我会把 3.7 看作一个很明显的信号：对 Anthropic 来说，post-training 已经从调整模型行为，走到了推动能力增长的核心位置。

r001.rationale: The response describes post-training as moving from behavior adjustment toward capability growth, but does not characterize this as a transition from small-scale patching to scalable post-training.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute earlier limits on post-training scale to the absence of a known way to scale it.

r003.rationale: It mentions verifiable feedback and coding tasks where feedback is easier to obtain, but does not identify sufficiently clear feedback signals as a condition of an environment suitable for scaling post-training.

r004.rationale: It does not identify the training environment itself as a strong source of data.
